n: This famous poem begins with its main idea: everything in life has its proper season. God has set a time for each human experience.
Life moves between opposites — birth and death, planting and harvesting. The poem pairs fourteen opposites, a number suggesting completeness (twice seven).
There are times for ending and times for healing, for tearing down and for building. Even painful seasons have their place in God’s order.
Grief and joy each have their time. Mourning and dancing are both part of a full human life.
Scattering and gathering stones may refer to clearing or building on farmland, and embracing and refraining to times of closeness and distance.

f.g: Possibly clearing a field of rocks, or spoiling an enemy’s field; the exact meaning is uncertain.

n: There are times to seek and gain, and times to let things go. Wisdom knows when to hold on and when to release.
Tearing clothing was a sign of mourning, and sewing it back a sign that grief had passed. There is also wisdom in knowing when to stay quiet and when to speak.

f.g: Tear — as people tore their clothes in grief.

n: Even love and hatred, war and peace, have their seasons in a fallen world. The poem ends on peace, a hopeful note.
After the poem, the Preacher returns to his question: if every season is set by God, what does a worker’s effort really add?
He has seen the burden of work God has given people to keep them occupied.
God makes everything beautiful in its proper time and has placed a longing for eternity in human hearts. Yet we can’t fully understand His work from start to finish.

f.g: Hebrew ‘olam — often “eternity”; God has put a sense of the eternal in people’s hearts.

n: The best thing people can do is to be glad and to do good while they live.
Being able to eat, drink, and find joy in one’s work is itself a gift from God.
What God does is permanent and complete; nothing can be added or removed. This is meant to fill people with reverent awe.

f.g: Reverence and awe toward God, not mere terror.

n: The patterns of the past recur, and God “seeks again” what has passed — He holds the past accountable and nothing slips from His notice.

f.g: Literally “seeks what has been driven away” — God calls the past back for judgment.

n: The Preacher saw corruption even in courts of justice: where righteousness should rule, wickedness had taken its place.
Yet he trusts that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, because God has a set time for every deed.
God allows these trials to test people and help them see that, left to themselves, they are as mortal as animals. It is a lesson in humility.

f.g: Test or sift; make plain what they are.

n: From an earthly view, humans and animals share the same fate: both breathe, and both die. In this sense people have no advantage.

f.g: Hebrew ruach — breath, wind, or spirit.

n: Both bodies return to the dust they came from, just as God told Adam.
He asks who can know for sure whether a human spirit goes up and an animal’s goes down. Later he affirms the spirit returns to God (12:7).

f.w: the spirit of man that goeth upward

n: So, he concludes, the best thing is to find joy in one’s own work, since no one can see what comes after this life from an earthly view.
